Empirical Research Plan  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1. Identification Strategy  
   Method: Sharp Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD) applied at the
   50-percent plurality threshold that determines which party is seated.  

   Justification  
   • The assignment rule is explicit and deterministic: the candidate (and
     hence the party) with the higher vote share wins the seat.  
   • For contests decided by very small margins, the identity of the winner is
     as-good-as random conditional on the running variable (Democratic vote
     margin).  
   • RDD allows us to:  
     – Test whether bare winners and losers are comparable on observables
       (density test, covariate balance).  
     – Produce a plausibly causal estimate of the “party incumbency
       advantage” (the effect of having won the seat) on subsequent political
       outcomes.  
   Difference-in-differences or IV designs are unnecessary because the
   statutory cutoff already furnishes a quasi-experimental design.

2. Treatment and Control  

   • Running variable:  
     m_i ≡ VoteShare_Dem,i – VoteShare_Rep,i  (in percentage points)  
     Positive m_i ⇒ Democratic plurality, negative m_i ⇒ Republican plurality.  

   • Cutoff: m_i = 0.  

   • Treatment definition (sharp RDD):  
     T_i = 1{m_i ≥ 0}.  “Treated” districts are those in which the Democratic
     candidate barely wins; control districts are those in which the Democrat
     barely loses (equivalently, the Republican barely wins).  

   • Event date / timing: the treatment is realized on Election Day of year t.
     Primary outcomes are measured in the next election (t+2), though
     contemporaneous and intermediate mechanisms (e.g., fundraising,
     recounts) are also studied.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

   A1. Continuity of potential outcomes: In the absence of treatment, the
       expectation of any outcome is continuous in m_i at zero.   
       Plausibility: The vote share is aggregated over hundreds of thousands
       of ballots; individual decisions are unlikely to coordinate precisely at
       the cutoff. No legal or administrative discontinuity other than seat
       allocation exists at zero.

   A2. No precise manipulation of the running variable: Candidates, parties,
       or election officials cannot sort exactly to just above or below the
       50 % mark.  
       Plausibility: While strategic effort is intense, the stochastic element
       of voter turnout and ballot counting at the precinct level dominates
       within ±0.5 p.p. Nevertheless, recount laws (often triggered at 0.5 %)
       could threaten this assumption and will be explicitly examined.

   A3. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA): The outcome in district i is not
       affected by the treatment status of other very close districts.  
       Plausibility: House districts are independent contests; spillovers are
       limited.

4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  

   Threat 1: Sorting / manipulation around recount thresholds (±0.5 %).  
   – Test: McCrary density test and separate density graphs around 0, ±0.5.  
   – Remedy: (i) Drop observations inside statutory automatic-recount
     windows; (ii) include recount indicator as covariate; (iii) use donut RDD
     that excludes ±0.25 p.p. window.

   Threat 2: Covariate discontinuities due to asymmetric national tides
   (e.g., Republicans win close seats in Democratic wave years).  
   – Test: RDD on predetermined covariates (presidential vote, demographics,
     CQ ratings).  
   – Remedy: Estimate local linear RDD with covariate adjustment; compute
     bias-corrected robust standard errors; present specification with
     county-cycle fixed effects to partial out national shocks.

   Threat 3: Heterogeneous treatment timing (special elections, recounts
   delaying seating).  
   – Remedy: Exclude special elections; verify that the delay between
     Election Day and certification is not discontinuous at m_i = 0; confirm
     same results using seating date as alternative running variable.

5. R Code Outline  

```r
# ---- 0. Packages ----
library(data.table)
library(fixest)     # fast estimators
library(rdrobust)   # RD inference
library(ggplot2)

# ---- 1. Load data ----
house <- fread("us_house_1942_2008.csv")   # one row per district-election

# ---- 2. Construct variables ----
house[, dem_margin := 100*(dem_votes - rep_votes)/(dem_votes + rep_votes)]
house[, treat := as.integer(dem_margin >= 0)]           # 1 = Democrat wins
house[, next_dem_share := shift(dem_share, type = "lead", n = 1),
      by = district_id]                                 # outcome in t+2
house[, next_dem_win   := as.integer(next_dem_share > 0.5)]

# Optional bandwidth (Calonico–Cattaneo–Titiunik optimal)
bw <- rdbwselect(next_dem_win, dem_margin)$bws[1]

# ---- 3. Main RD estimate (party advantage) ----
rd_main <- rdrobust(y = house$next_dem_win,
                    x = house$dem_margin,
                    p = 1, h = bw, covs = NULL)
summary(rd_main)

# ---- 4. Covariate balance check ----
cov_list <- c("incumbent_party", "cq_rating", "norm_pres_vote",
              "median_income", "black_share")
bal <- lapply(cov_list, function(v){
  rdrobust(y = house[[v]], x = house$dem_margin, p = 1, h = bw)
})

# ---- 5. Robustness: Donut RDD excluding ±0.25 p.p. ----
donut <- house[abs(dem_margin) > 0.25]
rd_donut <- rdrobust(y = donut$next_dem_win, x = donut$dem_margin,
                     p = 1, h = bw)
summary(rd_donut)
```

6. Expected Results  

Direction: Barely winning a seat should increase the party’s probability of
holding the seat in the next election.  
Magnitude: Prior work (Lee 2008, focusing on incumbency) finds ≈7–8 p.p.
We expect the “party advantage” to be slightly larger—roughly 10 percentage
points in win probability (equivalent to ≈5 p.p. in two-party vote share).

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RDD)  

C1: No visible manipulation of running variable density ………………… 1  
C2: Covariates smooth at cutoff ………………………………………………………… 1  
C3: Robust to bandwidth & polynomial choice …………………………………… 1  
C4: Correct functional form & standard errors ………………………………… 1  
C5: Placebo tests at fake cutoffs show no effects …………………………… 1  

Total: 5/5 – design appears internally valid subject to the empirical tests
described above.
